projects.title: Enterprise Private AI Platform
projects.short: A secure, on-premises AI platform providing private LLM inference, retrieval-augmented generation and document intelligence without dependency on external cloud providers.
projects.challenge: Delivering cloud-grade AI capability (chat, RAG, multi-user access) entirely within an organization's own infrastructure, with no data leaving the premises.
projects.businessValue: Keeps sensitive data in-house, removes per-token cloud inference costs, and gives IT full control over model versions, uptime and access policy.
objectives: Provide private large-language-model inference with no external API dependency.
Enable retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over an organization's internal documents.
Support multiple concurrent users with role-based access control.
Give administrators visibility into GPU utilization and model performance.
projects.problem: Organizations handling sensitive data (research, legal, engineering IP) increasingly want LLM-based productivity tools, but public cloud AI services require sending data outside the organization's security boundary, which is unacceptable for regulated or IP-sensitive workloads.
projects.solution: A self-hosted stack combining a GPU inference engine (vLLM/Ollama), a vector database (Qdrant) for document retrieval, PostgreSQL for application state, and a FastAPI backend exposing OpenAI-compatible endpoints, fronted by an Open WebUI interface, all running in containers on-premises.
projects.users: Internal engineering and research teams, legal/compliance staff handling confidential documents, and IT administrators managing model deployment.

businessDetail.operational: Eliminates per-seat/per-token SaaS AI subscriptions and keeps all prompts and documents inside the corporate network boundary.
businessDetail.cost: Upfront GPU hardware investment is offset over time versus recurring API costs at scale; exact break-even depends on usage volume and should be modeled per deployment.
businessDetail.productivity: Gives staff a ChatGPT-like assistant integrated with internal knowledge bases, reducing time spent searching documentation.
businessDetail.scalability: Additional GPU nodes can be added behind a load balancer as user count grows; model size can scale from 7B to 70B+ parameter classes depending on available VRAM.
businessDetail.security: All inference and document data stays within the organization's network; access is gated by role-based authentication.
businessDetail.impact: Positions IT as an enabler of safe AI adoption rather than a blocker, while retaining governance over what data the model can see.

architecture.overview: A three-tier architecture: a presentation tier (Open WebUI), an application/API tier (FastAPI + authentication), and an inference/data tier (vLLM on GPU nodes, Qdrant vector store, PostgreSQL).
components: vLLM / Ollama inference engine on CUDA GPUs
PostgreSQL for users, sessions, conversation history
architecture.dataflow: User query → FastAPI gateway → embedding model converts query → Qdrant similarity search retrieves relevant document chunks → context + query sent to vLLM-served LLM → response streamed back through gateway to Open WebUI.
architecture.integration: OpenAI-compatible API surface allows internal tools (scripts, IDE plugins, internal apps) to call the private model the same way they would call a public API, minimizing integration friction.

stackRationale.why: High-throughput GPU inference engine with continuous batching, giving better concurrent-user performance than naive model serving.
Purpose-built vector database with filtering support, needed for accurate RAG retrieval over internal documents.
Lightweight, async-capable Python framework well suited to building an OpenAI-compatible gateway with authentication middleware.
Containerization isolates each service (inference, DB, vector store) and simplifies reproducible deployment and upgrades.
Mature relational database for user accounts, audit logs and conversation metadata.

hardware.cpu: 16+ core server-grade CPU for the application/orchestration tier (model inference is GPU-bound).
hardware.gpu: One or more NVIDIA GPUs with 24GB+ VRAM for 7B–13B models; 48GB+ or multi-GPU for 30B–70B class models.
hardware.ram: 64GB+ system RAM recommended for host OS, container overhead, and embedding caches.
hardware.storage: NVMe SSD for model weights and vector index (model weights alone can range from 15GB–150GB depending on model size).
hardware.networking: 1GbE minimum for internal access; 10GbE recommended if serving many concurrent users or multiple GPU nodes.
hardware.recommended: Dual-GPU workstation or single GPU server node for pilot deployments; scales to multi-node with a load balancer for production.
hardware.note: All figures are estimated sizing guidance based on published vendor/model requirements, not benchmarked results from a live deployment.

software.os: Linux (Ubuntu Server LTS or Rocky Linux).
software.apis: OpenAI-compatible REST API exposed by the gateway for internal application integration.
software.monitoring: GPU utilization via nvidia-smi/DCGM exporter feeding Prometheus/Grafana.
software.automation: Ansible playbooks for repeatable provisioning of inference nodes.

roadmap.detail: Define user base, data sensitivity classification, target model sizes, and concurrency requirements.
Provision GPU server(s), install NVIDIA drivers/CUDA, configure base OS and networking.
Deploy containerized vLLM/Ollama, Qdrant, PostgreSQL and the FastAPI gateway; load initial model(s).
Connect Open WebUI, configure RBAC/authentication, ingest initial document set into the vector store.
Validate retrieval accuracy, measure tokens/sec throughput under concurrent load, test failover.
Finalize backup policy, access audit logging, and documented runbooks before general rollout.

security.authentication: Role-based login via the gateway, integrable with existing LDAP/Active Directory/FreeIPA.
security.authorization: Per-role access to specific knowledge bases and models.
security.network: Service exposed only on internal network segments; no public internet exposure by default.
security.backup: Regular backups of PostgreSQL metadata and the Qdrant vector index.
security.monitoring: Centralized logging of queries and access for audit purposes.
security.dr: Documented restore procedure for model weights, vector index and database snapshots.
security.ha: Optional multi-node inference with load balancing for environments requiring high availability.

testing: Functional test: verify RAG responses correctly cite ingested internal documents.
Load test: measure concurrent-user response latency at defined token-per-second targets.
Security test: confirm unauthorized roles cannot query restricted knowledge bases.
Failover test: validate graceful degradation if a GPU node becomes unavailable.
deliverables: Fully configured private AI platform with chat and RAG interface.
Documented API for internal application integration.
Admin dashboard for GPU and usage monitoring.
Operational runbook and backup/restore procedure.
future: Fine-tuning pipeline for domain-specific model adaptation.
Multi-tenant isolation for serving several departments independently.
Integration with enterprise SSO (SAML/OIDC).

projects.title: Distributed AI Training & Inference Cluster
projects.short: A scalable multi-GPU, multi-node computing infrastructure for distributed AI model training, fine-tuning and high-throughput inference.
projects.challenge: Coordinating multiple GPUs across multiple physical nodes so that training and inference workloads scale efficiently rather than being bottlenecked by communication overhead.
projects.businessValue: Allows an organization to train and serve larger models than a single machine could support, and to run many inference requests in parallel.
objectives: Enable distributed (multi-GPU, multi-node) model training and fine-tuning.
Provide high-throughput multi-GPU inference serving.
Implement fair GPU resource scheduling across users/teams.
Support model quantization to reduce memory footprint and increase throughput.
projects.problem: Modern deep learning models frequently exceed the memory and compute capacity of a single GPU, and single-node training is too slow for practical iteration cycles on large datasets.
projects.solution: A cluster of GPU-equipped nodes interconnected with high-speed networking, orchestrated by Slurm or Kubernetes, using PyTorch Distributed/DeepSpeed for parallel training and NCCL for efficient inter-GPU communication, with vLLM handling high-concurrency inference.
projects.users: ML research teams, data science groups, and engineering teams building or fine-tuning models at scale.

businessDetail.operational: Centralizes GPU capacity instead of siloed single-workstation setups, improving utilization across teams.
businessDetail.cost: Shared cluster scheduling improves GPU utilization versus idle dedicated workstations; exact savings depend on workload mix.
businessDetail.productivity: Shorter training iteration cycles through data/model parallelism across multiple GPUs.
businessDetail.scalability: Designed to grow from a few GPUs to many nodes by adding workers to the scheduler pool.
businessDetail.security: Workload isolation between users/teams via scheduler queues and namespaces.
businessDetail.impact: Builds internal capability to train and fine-tune models rather than relying solely on third-party model providers.

architecture.overview: A head/scheduler node coordinates jobs across a pool of GPU worker nodes, connected via high-bandwidth, low-latency networking for gradient synchronization.
components: GPU worker nodes with NVLink/PCIe GPUs
Shared/distributed storage for datasets and checkpoints
architecture.dataflow: Training job submitted to scheduler → scheduler allocates GPU workers → PyTorch Distributed/DeepSpeed partitions model/data across workers → gradients synchronized via NCCL each step → checkpoints written to shared storage.
architecture.integration: Inference workloads exposed via vLLM endpoints that can scale horizontally across the same GPU pool when training jobs are not consuming full capacity.

stackRationale.why: NVIDIA's collective communication library minimizes latency for gradient all-reduce operations across GPUs and nodes.
Provides memory-efficient optimizer sharding (ZeRO), enabling training of models larger than any single GPU's memory.
Mature schedulers for allocating shared GPU resources fairly across competing jobs and users.
Continuous batching and PagedAttention deliver significantly higher inference throughput than naive serving.

hardware.cpu: Server-grade multi-core CPUs per node to avoid CPU-side data loading bottlenecks.
hardware.gpu: Multiple NVIDIA data-center or high-end workstation GPUs per node (e.g. A100/H100/RTX class), ideally with NVLink.
hardware.ram: 256GB+ system RAM per node for large dataset staging and checkpoint buffering.
hardware.storage: High-throughput NVMe or parallel storage for dataset and checkpoint I/O.
hardware.networking: InfiniBand or 100GbE RDMA strongly recommended between nodes to avoid communication bottlenecks during distributed training.
hardware.recommended: Minimum viable cluster: 2 nodes × multi-GPU each; production-scale clusters typically use many more nodes depending on model size targets.
hardware.note: Hardware sizing is estimated guidance; actual throughput must be validated through benchmarking on the specific model/dataset.

software.os: Linux (Rocky Linux/Ubuntu Server) with NVIDIA driver and CUDA toolkit.
databases: Metadata/experiment tracking store (e.g. PostgreSQL) if experiment tracking is required.
software.apis: Job submission API/CLI via scheduler; inference API via vLLM.
software.monitoring: DCGM Exporter + Prometheus + Grafana for GPU utilization, memory and temperature.
software.automation: Ansible for node provisioning; scheduler-native job templates for recurring training runs.

roadmap.detail: Define target model sizes, number of concurrent users, and training vs inference capacity split.
Provision GPU nodes, install drivers/CUDA, set up high-speed interconnect.
Deploy scheduler, configure NCCL, install PyTorch Distributed/DeepSpeed.
Connect shared storage for datasets/checkpoints, integrate monitoring stack.
Run scaling tests measuring throughput vs GPU count; validate checkpoint/resume reliability.
Establish job queue policies, quotas and documented onboarding for research teams.

security.authentication: Centralized user authentication (LDAP/FreeIPA) integrated with the scheduler.
security.authorization: Scheduler queues/partitions to enforce per-team resource quotas.
security.network: Cluster interconnect isolated on a private/internal network segment.
security.backup: Checkpoint and dataset backup policy on shared storage.
security.monitoring: GPU health and job-level monitoring via Prometheus/Grafana.
security.dr: Checkpoint-based recovery for interrupted long-running training jobs.
security.ha: Scheduler high-availability configuration where continuous job submission uptime is required.

testing: Scaling test: measure training throughput as GPU count increases (strong/weak scaling).
Checkpoint/resume test: validate a killed job resumes correctly from the last checkpoint.
Inference load test: measure tokens/sec and latency under concurrent request load.
Quota enforcement test: confirm scheduler enforces per-team GPU limits.
deliverables: Operational multi-GPU, multi-node training and inference cluster.
Documented job submission templates for common training patterns.
Monitoring dashboards for GPU and job utilization.
Benchmark report comparing throughput at different scales.
future: Automated hyperparameter sweep orchestration.
Spot/preemptible job support for cost-efficient non-urgent training.
Model registry integration for versioned deployment from training to inference.

projects.title: AI-Powered Infrastructure Operations Platform (AIOps)
projects.short: An intelligent operations assistant that monitors infrastructure, analyzes logs, correlates alerts and helps administrators troubleshoot faster using an LLM grounded in real system data.
projects.challenge: Turning large volumes of noisy logs and metrics into actionable, trustworthy guidance without the AI inventing root causes it cannot verify.
projects.businessValue: Reduces mean-time-to-diagnosis for infrastructure incidents and lowers the cognitive load on on-call engineers.
objectives: Analyze server health signals and surface anomalies proactively.
Provide log intelligence that summarizes and correlates related log events.
Assist administrators with troubleshooting suggestions grounded in actual metrics/logs.
Support human-approved automated remediation rather than fully autonomous action.
projects.problem: Infrastructure teams are overwhelmed by the volume of logs, metrics and alerts generated by modern systems, and correlating signals across tools (Prometheus, Loki, Grafana) to find root cause is slow and manual.
projects.solution: An LLM-based assistant with retrieval-augmented access to a knowledge base of infrastructure documentation, historical incidents, and live metrics/log queries, exposed through a chat interface that administrators can query during incidents, with any remediation actions requiring explicit human approval before execution.
projects.users: Infrastructure/SRE teams, on-call engineers, and IT operations managers.

businessDetail.operational: Speeds up incident triage by correlating alerts and surfacing likely causes from historical patterns.
businessDetail.cost: Reduces engineer time spent manually cross-referencing dashboards and log sources during incidents.
businessDetail.productivity: Frees senior engineers from repetitive first-line triage work.
businessDetail.scalability: Knowledge base and monitoring integrations can expand as more systems are onboarded.
businessDetail.security: All remediation actions require human approval, preventing unsupervised changes to production systems.
businessDetail.impact: Builds institutional operational knowledge into a searchable, queryable system rather than relying on individual tribal knowledge.

architecture.overview: A retrieval-augmented assistant layered over existing observability tools (Prometheus, Loki, Grafana), with a FastAPI service mediating between the LLM, the vector knowledge base, and live metric/log queries.
components: Qdrant vector store for runbooks/documentation/past incidents
architecture.dataflow: Administrator asks a question or an alert fires → orchestration service gathers relevant metrics (Prometheus), logs (Loki) and knowledge base entries (Qdrant) → context assembled and sent to the LLM → response with suggested diagnosis/action returned → remediation, if any, requires explicit approval before an Ansible playbook executes.
architecture.integration: Integrates with existing Prometheus/Grafana/Loki deployments rather than replacing them, acting as an intelligence layer on top.

stackRationale.why: Grounds LLM responses in actual runbooks and historical incident data rather than relying purely on model memory, reducing hallucinated remediation steps.
Log aggregation designed to pair efficiently with Prometheus/Grafana, enabling unified correlation of metrics and logs.
Declarative, auditable automation suited to human-approved remediation playbooks.
Async-friendly orchestration layer to coordinate multiple data sources and the LLM call efficiently.

hardware.cpu: Standard server-grade CPU sufficient for orchestration service and data aggregation.
hardware.gpu: GPU required only if hosting the LLM locally (see Project 01); otherwise can call an existing private inference endpoint.
hardware.ram: 32GB+ for the orchestration/monitoring stack; more if hosting large log retention in Loki.
hardware.storage: Sufficient disk for Prometheus/Loki retention windows and the Qdrant knowledge base index.
hardware.networking: Standard internal LAN connectivity to all monitored systems.
hardware.recommended: Can run on a single mid-size server for small-to-medium infrastructure estates; scales horizontally for larger environments.
hardware.note: Sizing depends heavily on log/metric volume and retention policy; figures above are estimated starting points.

software.apis: Internal REST API for the chat assistant; existing Prometheus/Loki query APIs consumed internally.
software.monitoring: The platform monitors infrastructure, and is itself monitored for its own uptime and response latency.
software.automation: Ansible playbooks triggered only after explicit human approval of a suggested remediation.

roadmap.detail: Catalog existing monitoring tools, define scope of systems to onboard, and set approval workflow policy.
Ensure Prometheus/Loki/Grafana are deployed and collecting from target systems.
Deploy Qdrant, ingest existing runbooks/documentation, configure the orchestration service.
Connect the assistant to live metrics/log query endpoints and configure alert correlation rules.
Validate diagnosis suggestions against known past incidents; measure response relevance.
Finalize the human-approval workflow for remediation and document escalation paths.

security.authentication: Integrated with existing SSO/LDAP for administrator access.
security.authorization: Role-based restriction on who can approve automated remediation actions.
security.network: Internal-only access; no public exposure of the assistant interface.
security.backup: Backup of the knowledge base index and configuration.
security.monitoring: Audit log of every suggestion made and every action approved/executed.
security.dr: Documented recovery procedure for the orchestration service and knowledge base.
security.ha: Optional redundant deployment of the orchestration service for critical environments.

testing: Accuracy test: compare assistant diagnosis suggestions against known-cause historical incidents.
Safety test: confirm no remediation action executes without explicit human approval.
Latency test: measure time from query to grounded response under typical load.
Correlation test: verify related alerts across different systems are grouped correctly.
deliverables: Deployed AIOps assistant integrated with existing monitoring stack.
Searchable knowledge base of runbooks and historical incidents.
Human-approval workflow for any automated remediation.
Audit trail of assistant suggestions and executed actions.
future: Predictive anomaly detection using historical time-series patterns.
Automated post-incident report drafting.
Expansion to capacity planning recommendations.

projects.title: Enterprise HPC Cluster with Slurm Workload Manager
projects.short: A centralized, multi-user HPC computing cluster with Slurm-based job scheduling, shared storage and centralized authentication for research and engineering workloads.
projects.challenge: Providing fair, auditable, multi-user access to shared compute resources without jobs interfering with each other.
projects.businessValue: Replaces ad-hoc individual workstation computing with a shared, schedulable resource pool that improves overall utilization and fairness.
objectives: Deploy a head/login/compute node HPC architecture.
Implement Slurm-based job scheduling with partitions and queues.
Provide centralized authentication and user accounting.
Support CPU and GPU resource allocation per job.
projects.problem: Research and engineering teams often rely on individually-owned workstations for compute-intensive work, leading to poor resource utilization, no fair-share policy, and no centralized job history or accounting.
projects.solution: A Slurm-managed cluster with dedicated head (controller), login, and compute nodes, shared storage via NFS, centralized identity via FreeIPA/LDAP, and software environments managed through Spack for reproducibility.
projects.users: Research scientists, engineering simulation teams, and any group needing shared, scheduled access to compute resources.

businessDetail.operational: Converts scattered individual compute resources into a single schedulable pool with visibility into usage.
businessDetail.cost: Improves hardware utilization versus dedicated per-user workstations sitting idle outside business hours.
businessDetail.productivity: Users submit jobs instead of manually managing contention for shared machines.
businessDetail.scalability: Compute nodes can be added to the Slurm pool without disrupting running workloads.
businessDetail.security: Centralized authentication and per-user job isolation.
businessDetail.impact: Establishes the operational foundation (identity, scheduling, accounting) required before any advanced HPC workload (AI training, EDA compute, simulation) can run reliably at scale.

architecture.overview: Classic HPC topology: a controller node runs the Slurm scheduler, login nodes provide user access points, and compute nodes execute scheduled jobs, all sharing a common filesystem and identity service.
components: NFS shared storage for home directories and software
architecture.dataflow: User logs into login node → submits job via Slurm CLI → slurmctld schedules job to available compute node(s) based on partition/queue policy and requested resources → job executes with access to shared NFS storage → results returned to user's home directory.
architecture.integration: Spack-managed software stacks allow consistent application environments across all compute nodes without manual per-node installation.

stackRationale.why: Industry-standard HPC workload manager with mature support for partitions, fair-share scheduling, and GPU/CPU resource allocation.
Lightweight authentication mechanism required by Slurm for secure inter-node communication.
Centralizes user/group identity across all cluster nodes instead of managing local accounts per machine.
Purpose-built HPC package manager that handles complex scientific software dependency trees and multiple compiler/library versions cleanly.
Simple, well-understood shared storage suitable for home directories and moderate-scale shared software/data access.

hardware.cpu: Multi-core server CPUs on compute nodes sized to anticipated job parallelism (e.g. 32–128 cores per node).
hardware.gpu: Optional NVIDIA GPUs on select compute nodes for GPU-accelerated jobs.
hardware.ram: Sized per expected per-job memory needs; 128GB–512GB per compute node is a common range for mixed workloads.
hardware.storage: NFS server with sufficient capacity and IOPS for home directories and shared application installs.
hardware.networking: 1GbE/10GbE minimum; higher-bandwidth low-latency interconnect (InfiniBand/RoCE) recommended for MPI-heavy workloads (see Project 10).
hardware.recommended: Minimum viable cluster: 1 controller/login node + 2–4 compute nodes; production clusters scale to many more nodes.
hardware.note: These are planning-stage sizing estimates; actual requirements should be validated against target workloads before procurement.

software.os: Rocky Linux or RHEL across all nodes for long-term stability and enterprise support compatibility.
software.apis: Slurm CLI/REST API for job submission and status queries.
software.monitoring: Grafana dashboards fed by node_exporter and the Slurm exporter (see Project 05).
software.automation: Ansible playbooks for consistent node provisioning and configuration drift prevention.

roadmap.detail: Determine expected job types, user count, and partition/queue policy needs.
Provision controller, login and compute nodes; configure base OS and networking.
Install and configure Slurm, Munge, NFS, and FreeIPA/LDAP.
Deploy Spack environments, integrate accounting database, connect monitoring.
Submit test jobs across partitions; validate fair-share scheduling and resource limits.
Finalize user onboarding documentation and backup policy for shared storage.

security.authentication: Centralized via FreeIPA/LDAP; no local-only accounts on compute nodes.
security.authorization: Slurm partitions and QoS policies enforce per-group/user resource limits.
security.network: Cluster internal network isolated from general office network where practical.
security.backup: Regular backup of NFS home directories and the Slurm accounting database.
security.monitoring: Node health and job queue monitoring via Grafana.
security.dr: Documented rebuild procedure for the controller node and restoration of accounting data.
security.ha: Optional secondary Slurm controller for environments requiring scheduler high availability.

testing: Scheduling test: verify jobs are correctly queued and dispatched per partition policy.
Resource limit test: confirm per-user/group quotas are enforced.
Failover test: validate behavior when a compute node goes offline mid-job.
Software environment test: verify Spack-built applications run identically across all compute nodes.
deliverables: Operational Slurm-managed HPC cluster.
Documented job submission guide for end users.
Centralized authentication integrated across all nodes.
Accounting reports of cluster usage by user/group.
future: Integration with the HPC monitoring platform (Project 05) for full observability.
GPU partition expansion to support AI training workloads (Project 02).
Burst-to-cloud capability for peak demand periods.

projects.title: HPC Resource Management & Monitoring Platform
projects.short: A comprehensive monitoring dashboard providing full visibility into HPC cluster health: CPU, GPU, memory, storage, network and job queue utilization.
projects.challenge: Aggregating disparate metrics (compute, job scheduler, storage, network) into one coherent operational view without overwhelming administrators.
projects.businessValue: Gives administrators and leadership real visibility into cluster utilization, bottlenecks and capacity trends to justify infrastructure investment.
objectives: Monitor CPU, GPU, RAM, storage and network utilization across all cluster nodes.
Track Slurm job queue status and per-user/group utilization.
Provide historical analytics for capacity planning.
Alert administrators on cluster health anomalies.
projects.problem: Without centralized monitoring, HPC administrators lack visibility into which jobs are consuming resources, whether nodes are healthy, and where bottlenecks occur — making both troubleshooting and capacity planning guesswork.
projects.solution: A Prometheus + Grafana stack with purpose-built exporters (Node Exporter for system metrics, DCGM Exporter for GPU telemetry, Slurm Exporter for scheduler state) and Loki for log aggregation, presenting unified dashboards for cluster-wide and per-job visibility.
projects.users: HPC/cluster administrators, infrastructure managers, and capacity planning stakeholders.

businessDetail.operational: Reduces time spent manually SSH-ing into nodes to check status; gives a single pane of glass for cluster health.
businessDetail.cost: Identifies underutilized or over-provisioned resources, informing better future procurement decisions.
businessDetail.productivity: Speeds up troubleshooting of job failures and node issues through correlated metrics and logs.
businessDetail.scalability: Prometheus federation/remote-write patterns allow the monitoring stack to scale alongside cluster growth.
businessDetail.security: Read-only observability data; access controlled via Grafana authentication.
businessDetail.impact: Turns cluster operation from reactive firefighting into proactive, data-driven management.

architecture.overview: Exporters run on every node, scraped by a central Prometheus server; Grafana visualizes metrics, and Loki aggregates logs from the same nodes for correlated troubleshooting.
architecture.dataflow: Exporters expose metrics endpoints on each node → Prometheus scrapes them on an interval → Grafana queries Prometheus (and Loki for logs) to render dashboards → Alertmanager/Grafana alerting notifies administrators on threshold breaches.
architecture.integration: Designed to sit alongside the Slurm cluster (Project 04) as its observability layer, and can share infrastructure with the AIOps platform (Project 03).

stackRationale.why: Pull-based metrics collection well suited to dynamic HPC environments, with a powerful query language (PromQL) for analytics.
NVIDIA's own GPU telemetry exporter provides accurate utilization, memory, temperature and ECC error metrics not available from generic tools.
Exposes scheduler-specific metrics (queue depth, job states, partition utilization) that generic system exporters cannot provide.
Flexible dashboarding with strong Prometheus/Loki integration and built-in alerting.

hardware.cpu: Modest dedicated server for the monitoring stack (4–8 cores sufficient for small-to-mid clusters).
hardware.gpu: None required for the monitoring server itself; exporters run on existing GPU compute nodes.
hardware.ram: 16–32GB for Prometheus/Grafana/Loki depending on retention and cluster size.
hardware.storage: SSD storage sized to metric/log retention policy; long-term retention may require remote storage backends.
hardware.networking: Standard internal LAN access to scrape all cluster nodes.
hardware.recommended: Single monitoring server adequate for clusters up to roughly a few hundred nodes; larger environments may need Prometheus federation.
hardware.note: Storage sizing is an estimate dependent on metric cardinality and chosen retention window.

software.apis: Prometheus HTTP query API; Grafana API for dashboard provisioning as code.
software.monitoring: Self-monitoring of Prometheus/Grafana/Loki health is included to avoid blind spots.
software.automation: Ansible for exporter deployment across all nodes; dashboards provisioned as code for version control.

roadmap.detail: Define required metrics, retention policy, and alert thresholds with cluster administrators.
Provision the monitoring server and ensure network access to all cluster nodes.
Deploy Prometheus, Grafana, Loki and all exporters across the cluster.
Build dashboards for cluster-wide, per-node and per-job views; configure alerting rules.
Validate metric accuracy against known workloads; test alert firing and notification delivery.
Document dashboard usage and finalize alert escalation policy.

security.authentication: Grafana authentication integrated with centralized identity (LDAP/FreeIPA).
security.network: Monitoring traffic confined to internal network segments.
security.backup: Backup of Grafana dashboard definitions and Prometheus configuration.
security.monitoring: Includes monitoring of the monitoring stack itself.
security.dr: Documented rebuild procedure; metrics data loss during an outage is acceptable if dashboards/configs are preserved as code.
security.ha: Optional Prometheus high-availability pairing for critical environments.

testing: Metric accuracy test: compare exporter-reported values against manual checks (e.g. nvidia-smi vs DCGM exporter).
Alert test: trigger known threshold breaches and confirm notifications fire correctly.
Scale test: confirm scrape performance remains stable as node count grows.
Dashboard usability test: validate with actual administrators that key questions can be answered quickly.
deliverables: Fully deployed monitoring stack covering the entire HPC cluster.
Pre-built dashboards for cluster health, GPU utilization and job queue status.
Documented alerting rules and escalation paths.
Historical usage reports for capacity planning.
future: Predictive capacity forecasting based on historical trends.
Integration with the AIOps platform (Project 03) for intelligent alert correlation.
Cost-attribution reporting by team/project.

projects.title: Scientific Computing & Distributed Simulation Platform
projects.short: A high-performance scientific computing environment supporting parallel processing, distributed simulation and reproducible software environments for engineering and research workloads.
projects.challenge: Providing consistent, optimized compiler and numerical library environments across a cluster while supporting many different scientific applications with conflicting dependency needs.
projects.businessValue: Enables research and engineering teams to run computationally demanding simulations faster, with reproducible results across runs.
objectives: Support parallel computation via MPI (distributed) and OpenMP (shared-memory) models.
Provide optimized numerical libraries (BLAS/LAPACK/FFTW) for scientific applications.
Maintain reproducible, version-controlled software environments.
Benchmark application performance across different compiler/library configurations.
projects.problem: Scientific and engineering simulation codes (CFD, structural analysis, numerical modeling) require carefully tuned compiler toolchains and numerical libraries, and inconsistent environments across machines lead to non-reproducible results and wasted debugging time.
projects.solution: A dedicated scientific computing environment layered on the HPC cluster (Project 04), using Spack to manage multiple compiler (GCC, Intel oneAPI) and library (BLAS, LAPACK, FFTW) versions side-by-side, with MPI/OpenMP providing the parallel execution models applications need.
projects.users: Computational scientists, simulation engineers, and research groups running CFD, FEA, or other numerically intensive codes.

businessDetail.operational: Removes the burden of each researcher manually compiling and managing their own library stack.
businessDetail.cost: Optimized numerical libraries can meaningfully reduce simulation runtime, directly reducing compute-hour costs.
businessDetail.productivity: Reproducible environments mean results are comparable across runs and across team members.
businessDetail.scalability: New applications and library versions can be added via Spack without disrupting existing environments.
businessDetail.security: Environment modules are centrally managed and vetted rather than individually compiled by each user.
businessDetail.impact: Provides the numerical computing foundation that research credibility depends on — consistent, documented environments.

architecture.overview: Built on top of the HPC cluster's compute nodes, this platform adds a managed software environment layer (via Spack and environment modules) plus parallel runtime libraries (MPI/OpenMP) used by scientific applications.
components: Optimized numerical libraries: BLAS, LAPACK, FFTW
GCC and Intel oneAPI compiler toolchains
architecture.dataflow: Researcher loads a specific software environment (module load) → compiles or runs a simulation code linked against the chosen BLAS/LAPACK/FFTW build → MPI distributes the computation across cluster nodes → OpenMP parallelizes within each node's cores.
architecture.integration: Runs on the same Slurm-managed cluster (Project 04) and is monitored through the same observability platform (Project 05).

stackRationale.why: Allows multiple versions of compilers and libraries to coexist cleanly, which is essential since different scientific codes require different, sometimes conflicting, dependency versions.
Provides highly optimized math kernels (MKL) that often significantly outperform generic library builds on Intel hardware.
The standard high-performance library for fast Fourier transforms, used across many simulation and signal-processing codes.
Combining distributed-memory (MPI) and shared-memory (OpenMP) parallelism is the standard approach for scaling scientific codes efficiently across multi-node, multi-core clusters.

projects.title: Enterprise EDA Design & Compute Farm
projects.short: Centralized semiconductor design infrastructure providing shared EDA applications, PDK management, license services and secure design data storage for VLSI/IC design teams.
projects.challenge: Managing expensive, license-gated commercial EDA tools and sensitive design IP (PDKs, GDS files) across a multi-user engineering team securely and efficiently.
projects.businessValue: Centralizes costly EDA tool licenses and design data, improving utilization and reducing IP exposure risk compared to scattered individual workstation installs.
objectives: Centralize EDA application installation and version management.
Manage shared Process Design Kit (PDK) access securely.
Operate centralized FLEXlm license servers for commercial EDA tools.
Enforce strict access control over sensitive design data.
projects.problem: Semiconductor design teams depend on expensive, license-controlled commercial EDA tools (Cadence Virtuoso, Spectre, Xcelium, etc.) and highly sensitive foundry PDKs; running these per-workstation leads to license contention, inconsistent tool versions, and weak control over where design IP physically resides.
projects.solution: A centralized compute farm model: EDA applications and PDKs are installed once on shared, access-controlled storage, FLEXlm license servers are centralized, and engineers access the environment via remote sessions rather than copying design data to local machines.
projects.users: IC/VLSI design engineers, verification engineers, physical design teams, and CAD/EDA infrastructure administrators.

businessDetail.operational: Removes per-workstation EDA tool installation and version-mismatch issues across a design team.
businessDetail.cost: Centralized licensing improves FLEXlm license utilization versus statically assigning licenses per seat.
businessDetail.productivity: Engineers get consistent tool versions and PDK access without manual setup per machine.
businessDetail.scalability: Additional compute nodes can be added to the farm as design team headcount or project load grows.
businessDetail.security: Design data and PDKs never need to leave centralized, access-controlled storage, reducing IP leakage risk.
businessDetail.impact: Establishes the infrastructure foundation required before automation like Project 08 (license-aware scheduling) or Project 09 (RTL-to-GDSII pipelines) can be layered on top.

architecture.overview: A compute farm of Linux servers running EDA applications against centrally-stored PDKs and design libraries over NFS, with FLEXlm license servers brokering tool access and LDAP/Active Directory providing identity.
components: Centralized NFS storage for PDKs and design libraries
Remote access layer (e.g. VNC/NX/Citrix-style remote desktop) for GUI tools like Virtuoso
architecture.dataflow: Engineer authenticates via LDAP/AD → connects to a compute node via remote session → loads project environment pointing to centralized PDK/library paths on NFS → runs Virtuoso/Spectre/Xcelium, which checks out a license from the FLEXlm server for the session duration → design data remains on central storage throughout.
architecture.integration: Provides the base platform that license-aware scheduling (Project 08) and automated digital flows (Project 09) build upon.

stackRationale.why: The standard license management protocol used by virtually all major commercial EDA vendors (Cadence, Synopsys, Siemens); centralizing it is mandatory, not optional, for these tools.
Provides a shared filesystem view of PDKs and libraries across all compute nodes, which EDA tools expect for consistent path references.
Enterprise design teams require centralized, auditable identity management, especially given IP sensitivity.
The near-universal operating system target for commercial EDA tool qualification and support.

hardware.cpu: High single-thread performance and large core counts for simulation/synthesis jobs; EDA tools vary widely in parallelism support.
hardware.gpu: Generally not required for traditional EDA tools, though some newer simulation/ML-assisted EDA features may benefit from GPU acceleration.
hardware.ram: Large RAM per node (128GB–1TB+) as tools like Virtuoso/Spectre/Tempus can be memory-intensive on large designs.
hardware.storage: High-capacity, high-IOPS centralized storage for PDKs, libraries and active design data.
hardware.networking: 10GbE minimum between compute nodes and storage to avoid NFS becoming a bottleneck for large design databases.
hardware.recommended: Minimum viable farm: license server + 2–4 compute nodes; production farms scale with design team size and project parallelism needs.
hardware.note: EDA tool resource requirements vary significantly by vendor and tool; figures are general planning estimates, not vendor-certified specs.

software.os: Linux distribution matching vendor-qualified support matrices for the specific EDA tool versions in use.
software.databases: Not typically required beyond license server state and LDAP/AD directory data.
software.apis: Vendor tool CLIs/APIs for scripted flows (e.g. Virtuoso SKILL, Tcl interfaces for synthesis/verification tools).
software.monitoring: License usage and compute node health monitoring (see Project 08 for dedicated license analytics).
software.automation: Ansible for consistent compute node provisioning and PDK/library path configuration.

roadmap.detail: Catalog required EDA tools, license counts, and design team size/growth expectations.
Provision compute nodes, centralized storage, and license server infrastructure.
Install EDA applications, configure FLEXlm license servers, set up PDK/library storage structure.
Connect LDAP/AD authentication, configure remote access sessions, set storage permissions.
Validate tool launches, license checkout/release behavior, and design data access permissions.
Document engineer onboarding process and finalize design data backup/retention policy.

security.authentication: Centralized via LDAP/Active Directory; no local tool access without directory authentication.
security.authorization: Fine-grained NFS/filesystem permissions restricting PDK and design library access by project/team.
security.network: EDA farm network segment isolated from general corporate network; remote access brokered rather than direct exposure.
security.backup: Regular backup of design libraries and PDK repositories, with versioning for design data.
security.monitoring: Access logging for design data and license checkout activity.
security.dr: Documented recovery procedure for license servers and centralized storage.
security.ha: Optional redundant license servers and storage for environments where design downtime is costly.

testing: License checkout test: confirm tools correctly acquire and release FLEXlm licenses.
Access control test: verify project-level storage permissions correctly restrict unauthorized PDK/library access.
Remote session test: validate GUI tool (e.g. Virtuoso) performance over the remote access layer.
Failover test: validate behavior when the primary license server is unavailable (if redundant licensing configured).
