Documented PDK and design library storage structure.
Operational FLEXlm license infrastructure.
Engineer onboarding and remote access guide.
future: License-aware job scheduling layer (Project 08).
Integration with automated digital design flows (Project 09).
Expanded remote access for distributed/international design teams.

projects.title: EDA Workload Scheduling & License Optimization System
projects.short: An intelligent scheduling and analytics platform that correlates compute job scheduling with EDA license availability to reduce license bottlenecks and improve utilization visibility.
projects.challenge: EDA jobs frequently queue or fail not because compute is unavailable, but because license tokens are exhausted — a resource dimension traditional schedulers don't natively understand.
projects.businessValue: Reduces wasted engineer time waiting on license availability and provides data to justify (or avoid) purchasing additional costly EDA licenses.
objectives: Monitor real-time license availability and usage across all FLEXlm-managed EDA tools.
Make job scheduling license-aware so jobs aren't dispatched to wait indefinitely on unavailable licenses.
Provide per-user/team license utilization analytics.
Identify license bottlenecks to inform purchasing or reallocation decisions.
projects.problem: Standard HPC schedulers (like Slurm) allocate CPU/GPU/memory but have no native concept of software license availability, so EDA jobs can be dispatched to compute resources only to immediately stall waiting for a FLEXlm license token, wasting both compute allocation and engineer time.
projects.solution: A Python-based middleware layer that polls FLEXlm license server status, exposes license availability as a schedulable resource to Slurm (via Slurm's licenses resource feature or a custom plugin), and logs usage data to PostgreSQL for Grafana-based analytics and bottleneck reporting.
projects.users: EDA infrastructure administrators, CAD/IT managers responsible for license budget decisions, and design engineers submitting license-gated jobs.

businessDetail.operational: Prevents jobs from occupying compute slots while stalled on unavailable licenses, improving overall farm throughput.
businessDetail.cost: Usage analytics reveal whether license bottlenecks are chronic (justifying purchase) or occasional (justifying better scheduling instead), avoiding unnecessary license spend.
businessDetail.productivity: Engineers get more predictable job start times since licenses are checked before dispatch, not after.
businessDetail.scalability: Additional license pools/tools can be added to the monitoring and scheduling layer incrementally.
businessDetail.security: Read-only license server queries; no changes to the underlying FLEXlm authorization model.
businessDetail.impact: Turns license management from a reactive support issue into a data-driven capacity planning function.

architecture.overview: A middleware service polls FLEXlm license servers for real-time token availability, exposes this data via REST API and to Slurm as a licenses resource, and persists historical usage to PostgreSQL for analytics dashboards.
components: REST API (for programmatic license status queries)
architecture.dataflow: Middleware service queries FLEXlm status periodically → updates Slurm's configured license resource counts → Slurm only dispatches license-gated jobs when both compute and license resources are available → usage snapshots logged to PostgreSQL → Grafana visualizes utilization trends and bottlenecks.
architecture.integration: Sits on top of the EDA compute farm (Project 07), adding an intelligence layer without requiring changes to how engineers submit jobs.

stackRationale.why: Slurm natively supports tracking arbitrary 'license' resources, making it the natural integration point rather than building a scheduler from scratch.
Flexible for writing FLEXlm status parsers (lmstat output) and REST middleware quickly and maintainably.
Reliable relational storage for time-series-like usage logs that need relational querying (by user, tool, project).
Reuses the same observability stack as other HPC projects (Project 05) for consistency and lower operational overhead.

hardware.cpu: Lightweight — the middleware service itself has minimal compute requirements (a few cores sufficient).
hardware.ram: 8–16GB typically sufficient for the middleware and database services.
hardware.storage: Modest storage for PostgreSQL historical usage logs; grows slowly over time.
hardware.networking: Standard internal LAN access to FLEXlm license servers and the Slurm controller.
hardware.recommended: Can run as a single lightweight service, potentially co-located with existing monitoring infrastructure (Project 05).
hardware.note: Resource needs are minimal relative to the compute farm itself; this is a coordination layer, not a compute-heavy service.

software.os: Linux, matching the EDA compute farm environment.
databases: PostgreSQL for historical license usage records.
software.apis: REST API exposing current and historical license availability for dashboards and user-facing tools.
software.monitoring: Grafana dashboards for license utilization trends and bottleneck alerts.
software.automation: Scheduled polling jobs; alerting rules for sustained license exhaustion.

roadmap.detail: Inventory all FLEXlm-managed tools and license pool sizes requiring monitoring.
Provision the middleware service host and confirm network access to license servers.
Build and deploy the FLEXlm polling service; configure Slurm license resources.
Connect PostgreSQL logging and Grafana dashboards; expose REST API for status queries.
Validate scheduling behavior under simulated license exhaustion; verify analytics accuracy against known usage.
Document bottleneck reporting process and finalize alert thresholds with CAD management.

security.authentication: Middleware service uses read-only, scoped access to query FLEXlm status.
security.authorization: Dashboard access role-restricted to CAD/IT administrators and management.
security.network: Middleware communicates only with internal license servers and the Slurm controller.
security.backup: PostgreSQL usage history backed up on a standard schedule.
security.monitoring: Self-monitoring to ensure the polling service itself stays healthy and current.
security.dr: Service can be redeployed quickly from version-controlled configuration if lost.
security.ha: Optional redundant polling service for environments where license visibility must stay continuous.

testing: Polling accuracy test: compare middleware-reported license counts against raw lmstat output.
Scheduling test: confirm Slurm withholds license-gated jobs when tokens are exhausted.
Analytics test: validate historical usage reports against known usage windows.
Alert test: confirm sustained license exhaustion triggers the configured alert.
deliverables: License-aware job scheduling integrated with the existing Slurm/EDA farm.
Historical license utilization dashboards and bottleneck reports.
REST API for programmatic license status queries.
Documented recommendations process for license purchase decisions.
future: Predictive license demand forecasting based on project pipeline.
Per-project cost-attribution reporting for license usage.
Integration with the AIOps platform (Project 03) for intelligent bottleneck alerts.

projects.title: Automated RTL-to-GDSII Semiconductor Design Pipeline
projects.short: An automated open-source digital design flow taking Verilog RTL through synthesis, place-and-route and timing analysis to final GDSII layout, built on OpenROAD/OpenLane tooling.
projects.challenge: Chaining together many independent, complex EDA stages (synthesis, floorplanning, placement, CTS, routing, timing, DRC) into a single reliable, repeatable automated flow.
projects.businessValue: Provides a low-cost, open-source alternative digital design flow useful for education, prototyping and open-source silicon projects, distinct from costly commercial flows.
objectives: Automate the full RTL-to-GDSII flow using open-source digital design tools.
Validate functional correctness via simulation before synthesis.
Perform synthesis, floorplanning, placement, clock tree synthesis and routing.
Produce a DRC-clean GDSII layout targeting an open PDK (e.g. SkyWater 130nm).
projects.problem: Commercial RTL-to-GDSII flows (Cadence/Synopsys) are powerful but expensive and license-gated, making them inaccessible for education, open-source hardware projects, and rapid low-risk prototyping; an automated open-source alternative fills this gap.
projects.solution: An OpenLane-orchestrated flow chaining Yosys (synthesis), OpenROAD (floorplanning, placement, CTS, routing), OpenSTA (static timing analysis), and Magic/KLayout (DRC/LVS and layout viewing), targeting the open SkyWater 130nm PDK, with functional verification via Verilator/Icarus Verilog prior to synthesis.
projects.users: Digital IC design students/educators, open-source silicon hobbyist projects, and engineering teams prototyping designs before committing to costly commercial flows.

businessDetail.operational: Provides a repeatable, scriptable design flow that doesn't depend on commercial license availability.
businessDetail.cost: Zero tool licensing cost versus commercial EDA suites, at the tradeoff of reduced feature set and typically older/larger process nodes.
businessDetail.productivity: Full automation means a design can go from RTL to layout with minimal manual intervention once the flow is configured.
businessDetail.scalability: The same flow structure can be adapted to other open PDKs as they become available.
businessDetail.security: All tooling is open-source and can be fully audited; no external license server dependency.
businessDetail.impact: Builds deep, transferable understanding of the full digital design flow — valuable both for training engineers and for genuine open-source chip projects.

architecture.overview: A staged pipeline orchestrated by OpenLane, where each stage consumes the previous stage's output: RTL → synthesized netlist → floorplan → placed design → clock-tree-inserted design → routed design → GDSII, with verification and timing checks interleaved.
architecture.dataflow: Verilog RTL → functional simulation (Verilator/Icarus) confirms correctness → Yosys synthesizes RTL to a gate-level netlist using PDK standard cells → OpenROAD performs floorplanning, placement and clock tree synthesis → OpenROAD routing produces a fully routed design → OpenSTA verifies timing closure → Magic/KLayout perform DRC/LVS and generate final GDSII.
architecture.integration: Can run as standalone scripted jobs on the HPC cluster (Project 04) compute nodes, since these are open-source CLI tools with no license server dependency.

stackRationale.why: Provides pre-built orchestration gluing together Yosys/OpenROAD/Magic into a coherent flow, avoiding the need to hand-script every stage transition.
The leading open-source place-and-route engine, actively maintained and capable of producing tape-out-quality results for supported open PDKs.
The most mature fully open-source PDK available, enabling genuinely manufacturable (via efabless/Skywater shuttle programs) open-source silicon.
The standard open-source RTL synthesis tool, well integrated with the rest of the open EDA ecosystem.

hardware.cpu: Multi-core CPU for parallelizable stages (placement/routing can be CPU-intensive on larger designs).
hardware.gpu: Not required — the open-source digital flow tooling (Yosys/OpenROAD/Magic) is CPU-based.
hardware.ram: 16–64GB depending on design size; larger designs with more standard cells need more memory for placement/routing.
hardware.storage: Moderate storage for PDK files, intermediate design databases (netlists, DEF/LEF files) and GDSII outputs.
hardware.networking: Standard LAN sufficient; no special interconnect requirements for single-node flow execution.
hardware.recommended: A single capable workstation/server node is typically sufficient for small-to-moderate digital designs on this flow.
hardware.note: Runtime and resource needs scale with design complexity (cell/gate count); figures are general estimates for small-to-moderate designs.

software.os: Linux (Ubuntu is the most commonly documented/tested base for OpenLane).
dependencies: Docker (OpenLane is commonly distributed as a container)
software.services: Not applicable — this is a batch/pipeline flow rather than a persistent service.
software.databases: Not applicable; design data is file-based (Verilog, DEF/LEF, GDSII).
software.apis: OpenLane/OpenROAD provide Tcl/Python scripting interfaces for flow customization.
software.monitoring: Flow run logs reviewed for stage success/failure and timing/DRC violations.
software.automation: Fully scriptable end-to-end via OpenLane configuration files, suitable for CI-style automated runs per RTL change.

roadmap.detail: Define target design(s), target PDK, and performance/area goals.
Provision a Linux host/container environment and install OpenLane/OpenROAD toolchain.
Configure PDK setup, flow configuration files, and design-specific constraints (SDC).
Integrate RTL simulation (Verilator/Icarus) as a pre-synthesis verification gate in the flow.
Run the full flow on representative test designs; verify timing closure and DRC-clean GDSII output.
Document the flow configuration and known limitations versus commercial tools for future users.

security.authentication: Not applicable in a single-user flow context; relevant only if hosted as a shared service.
security.authorization: File-level permissions on design data if shared across a team.
security.network: No external network dependency once PDK and tools are locally installed.
security.backup: Version control (git) for RTL and flow configuration; backup of generated GDSII outputs.
security.monitoring: Flow run logs retained for debugging failed stages.
security.dr: Flow is fully reproducible from version-controlled RTL and configuration, simplifying recovery.
security.ha: Not applicable — this is a batch pipeline, not a continuously available service.

testing: Functional test: RTL simulation must pass before synthesis proceeds.
Timing test: OpenSTA must report timing closure against the target clock constraint.
DRC/LVS test: Magic-generated layout must pass design rule and layout-vs-schematic checks.
Regression test: confirm flow produces consistent results across repeated runs of the same RTL.
deliverables: Automated, reproducible RTL-to-GDSII flow for the target open PDK.
DRC-clean GDSII layout output for completed designs.
Timing and DRC/LVS verification reports.
Documented flow configuration for reuse on future designs.
future: Extension to additional open PDKs as they mature.
CI-integrated flow triggering automatically on RTL commits.
Comparison benchmarking against commercial flow results on the same design where feasible.
projects.note: This project clearly distinguishes open-source digital design tooling (Yosys/OpenROAD/Magic/OpenLane, used here) from commercial EDA platforms (Cadence/Synopsys, used in Projects 07–08) — the two serve different purposes: open-source flows for education, prototyping and open silicon; commercial flows for production-grade advanced-node analog/mixed-signal and full-custom design.

projects.title: High-Speed Data Center Networking Infrastructure
projects.short: A scalable, high-throughput network fabric designed to support AI, HPC, EDA and general enterprise workloads with appropriate redundancy and traffic engineering.
projects.challenge: Selecting and designing the right networking technology (Ethernet vs RoCE vs InfiniBand) for different workload types sharing the same data center.
projects.businessValue: Prevents network bandwidth from becoming the limiting factor for AI training, HPC jobs and storage access, protecting the investment made in compute and storage hardware.
objectives: Design a tiered network topology (core/access) suitable for mixed workloads.
Provide high-speed server connectivity appropriate to each workload type.
Implement VLAN segmentation and link redundancy.
Support RDMA-based low-latency networking where required (AI/HPC).
projects.problem: A data center hosting AI training, HPC simulation, EDA compute and general enterprise services has very different networking needs per workload: AI/HPC often needs ultra-low-latency RDMA, while general services need reliable, segmented Ethernet — a single flat network design serves neither well.
projects.solution: A tiered network architecture with a high-speed core, workload-appropriate access layer technology (RoCE or InfiniBand for AI/HPC racks, standard high-speed Ethernet for general enterprise racks), VLAN segmentation for traffic isolation, and link aggregation (LACP) plus redundant paths for reliability.
projects.users: AI/HPC/EDA compute clusters requiring low-latency interconnect, enterprise IT services requiring reliable general-purpose networking, and network administrators managing the overall fabric.

businessDetail.operational: Matches network investment to actual workload needs instead of over- or under-provisioning uniformly.
businessDetail.cost: Avoids costly InfiniBand/RoCE deployment where standard Ethernet would suffice, while ensuring it's available where genuinely needed.
businessDetail.productivity: Prevents network bottlenecks from undermining the performance of expensive compute/storage hardware.
businessDetail.scalability: Tiered design allows new racks/pods to be added to whichever tier matches their workload profile.
businessDetail.security: VLAN segmentation isolates workload traffic types from each other.
businessDetail.impact: Provides the networking backbone that every other infrastructure project (AI, HPC, EDA, storage) ultimately depends on for performance.

architecture.overview: A core-and-access topology where the core provides high-speed inter-rack connectivity, and access-layer technology is chosen per workload: RDMA-capable RoCE or InfiniBand for AI/HPC racks, and standard 10/25/40/100GbE for general enterprise and EDA racks.
components: RDMA-capable NICs for AI/HPC nodes (RoCE) or InfiniBand HCAs
LACP link aggregation for redundancy and bandwidth
architecture.dataflow: Server traffic enters the access switch for its rack → access switch forwards to the core based on destination → core routes between racks/pods → for RDMA-enabled workloads, data paths bypass the standard TCP/IP stack for lower latency and CPU overhead.
architecture.integration: Underpins every compute-heavy project in this portfolio (Projects 02, 04, 06, 09) and the parallel storage platform (Project 13), which both depend on this networking layer for performance.

stackRationale.why: Delivers InfiniBand-like low latency and CPU-bypass benefits while running over standard Ethernet infrastructure, lowering cost versus a dedicated InfiniBand fabric.
Still the gold standard for the lowest possible latency and highest message rates in the most demanding HPC/AI training scenarios, at higher cost and specialized hardware requirements.
Standard link aggregation protocol providing both bandwidth increase and redundancy without proprietary vendor lock-in.
Isolates different traffic types (management, storage, compute, general enterprise) on shared physical infrastructure for both security and traffic engineering reasons.

hardware.cpu: Not primarily CPU-bound; relevant CPU consideration is NIC offload capability reducing host CPU overhead.
hardware.gpu: Not applicable directly, though GPU-to-GPU traffic (e.g. multi-node AI training) is a primary driver for RDMA network design.
hardware.ram: Not a primary sizing factor for networking equipment; switch buffer memory is vendor-specific.
hardware.storage: Not applicable to networking equipment itself.
hardware.networking: Core: 100GbE+ backbone recommended for mixed-workload data centers. AI/HPC access: RoCE-capable 100GbE+ NICs or InfiniBand HDR/NDR. General enterprise access: 10GbE/25GbE commonly sufficient.
hardware.recommended: Design should be workload-driven: start with a core sized for aggregate bandwidth needs, then size each access tier to its specific workload's latency/throughput requirements.
hardware.note: Exact speed/technology selection depends on specific workload profiling; figures given are general industry guidance, not a benchmarked design for a specific deployment.

software.os: Switch OS (vendor-specific, e.g. Cumulus Linux or vendor NOS) and Linux networking stack on servers.
dependencies: RDMA drivers/libraries (e.g. libibverbs) on RDMA-enabled hosts.
services: Network monitoring/telemetry agents on switches and servers.
software.databases: Not applicable directly; network telemetry may feed into Prometheus/Grafana (Project 05).
software.apis: Switch management APIs (vendor-specific) for configuration automation.
software.monitoring: Network monitoring tools tracking link utilization, error rates, and latency per segment.
software.automation: Network configuration automation (e.g. Ansible network modules) for consistent VLAN/LACP configuration.

roadmap.detail: Profile workload types (AI/HPC/EDA/enterprise) and their bandwidth/latency requirements.
Select core/access switch hardware and cabling (fiber optics) matching the target speeds.
Configure VLANs, LACP bonds, and RDMA/RoCE or InfiniBand settings per access tier.
Connect compute/storage clusters to their appropriate access tier; validate end-to-end connectivity.
Run throughput benchmarks (e.g. iperf3, RDMA bandwidth/latency tools) per tier against design targets.
Document the network topology and finalize redundancy/failover testing.

security.authentication: Switch management access secured via centralized authentication (RADIUS/TACACS+ or LDAP where supported).
security.authorization: VLAN-based segmentation restricting which traffic types can reach which network zones.
security.network: Management network separated from data-plane traffic.
security.backup: Switch configuration backups maintained and version-controlled.
security.monitoring: Continuous link utilization and error-rate monitoring to detect degradation before failure.
security.ha: Redundant core switches and multi-path access connectivity to avoid single points of failure.

testing: Throughput test: validate each tier achieves its designed bandwidth under load (e.g. iperf3).
Latency test: measure RDMA/RoCE/InfiniBand latency against expected figures for the chosen technology.
Failover test: confirm traffic reroutes correctly when a link or switch fails.
Segmentation test: verify VLAN isolation prevents unintended cross-traffic between zones.
deliverables: Documented network topology diagram and VLAN/segmentation plan.
Operational core/access network fabric sized to workload needs.
Benchmark report validating achieved throughput/latency per tier.
Network configuration backup and change management process.
future: Migration path to higher speeds (200GbE/400GbE) as workload demands grow.
Software-defined networking (SDN) overlay for more dynamic traffic engineering.
Expanded telemetry integration with the AIOps platform (Project 03).
projects.whenToUse: Standard Ethernet is appropriate for general enterprise traffic and workloads tolerant of typical TCP/IP latency. RoCE is appropriate when RDMA-level latency/CPU-bypass benefits are needed but the organization wants to stay on Ethernet-based infrastructure for cost/compatibility reasons. InfiniBand is appropriate for the most demanding HPC/AI training clusters where the lowest possible latency and highest message rates justify its specialized hardware and operational requirements.

projects.title: Enterprise Network Security & Zero Trust Architecture
projects.short: A secure enterprise networking design built on Zero Trust principles: centralized identity, network segmentation, firewall policy, VPN access and continuous security monitoring.
projects.challenge: Moving from implicit trust within the network perimeter to a model where every access request is explicitly authenticated and authorized, without breaking usability for legitimate users.
projects.businessValue: Reduces the blast radius of any single compromised credential or device, and provides auditable, centralized security visibility across the enterprise network.
objectives: Implement network segmentation aligned with Zero Trust principles.
Centralize authentication and authorization across all network resources.
Deploy firewall policies, VPN access and intrusion detection/prevention.
Establish centralized security logging and auditing.
projects.problem: Traditional perimeter-based security assumes that anything inside the network boundary can be trusted, but this leaves organizations highly exposed once any single internal device or credential is compromised, since lateral movement is largely unrestricted.
projects.solution: A Zero Trust-aligned architecture where network segments are strictly firewalled from each other by default, all access requires explicit authentication against centralized identity (FreeIPA/Active Directory), remote access uses modern VPN technology (WireGuard), and Wazuh plus IDS/IPS provide continuous security monitoring and centralized logging.
projects.users: Security/network administrators, compliance officers, and any staff requiring secure remote or segmented internal access.

businessDetail.operational: Limits lateral movement of any compromised device/credential by default, rather than relying solely on perimeter defenses.
businessDetail.cost: Primarily built on open-source tooling (pfSense/OPNsense, WireGuard, Wazuh), minimizing licensing costs relative to commercial security appliances.
businessDetail.productivity: Modern VPN (WireGuard) provides fast, low-overhead secure remote access without the performance penalties of older VPN technologies.
businessDetail.scalability: Segmentation and policy rules can be extended as new network zones or user groups are added.
businessDetail.security: Directly improves the organization's security posture through defense-in-depth principles.
businessDetail.impact: Provides the security foundation that protects every other infrastructure project in this portfolio — AI platforms, HPC clusters, EDA design data, and storage systems all depend on this layer for protection.

architecture.overview: A segmented network where firewalls (pfSense/OPNsense) enforce policy between VLANs, all user/device authentication routes through centralized identity, remote users connect via WireGuard VPN into specific authorized segments only, and Wazuh/IDS/IPS continuously monitor for anomalous activity.
architecture.dataflow: User/device requests access → authenticates against FreeIPA/Active Directory → firewall policy evaluates whether the authenticated identity is authorized for the requested network segment → if remote, WireGuard VPN establishes an encrypted tunnel scoped to authorized segments only → all access and security events logged centrally and monitored by Wazuh/IDS-IPS.
architecture.integration: Applies as a security overlay across all other infrastructure projects — AI platforms, HPC/EDA compute farms, and storage systems all sit behind this segmentation and monitoring layer.

stackRationale.why: Modern VPN protocol with a much smaller codebase and better performance than legacy IPsec/OpenVPN, simplifying both security auditing and user experience.
Mature, well-documented open-source firewall platforms capable of enterprise-grade policy enforcement without commercial licensing costs.
Open-source security monitoring providing SIEM-like log correlation and alerting, suited to centralizing visibility across a segmented network.
Centralized identity is the foundation Zero Trust is built on — every access decision depends on confidently knowing who/what is making the request.

hardware.cpu: Firewall appliances sized to expected throughput; software firewalls (pfSense/OPNsense) on commodity server hardware scale with core count and NIC offload capability.
hardware.ram: 16–32GB typical for firewall/VPN gateway hosts depending on concurrent session/tunnel count.
hardware.storage: Sufficient storage for centralized log retention (Wazuh/SIEM data can grow significantly depending on retention policy).
hardware.networking: Multiple NICs per firewall host to physically or logically separate zones; throughput sized to inter-zone traffic volume.
hardware.recommended: A dedicated firewall appliance or server per major site/zone boundary, with centralized logging infrastructure sized to total log volume across all zones.
hardware.note: Sizing is estimated guidance; actual throughput and log volume requirements should be measured against real traffic patterns.

software.os: pfSense/OPNsense (FreeBSD-based) for firewall appliances; Linux for Wazuh/logging infrastructure.
dependencies: IDS/IPS engine (e.g. Suricata, commonly integrated with pfSense/OPNsense)
databases: Wazuh's indexer (typically OpenSearch-based) for security event storage.
software.apis: Firewall management APIs for configuration automation; Wazuh API for programmatic security event queries.
software.monitoring: Wazuh dashboards for security event visibility; IDS/IPS alerting for active threat detection.
software.automation: Infrastructure-as-code approach to firewall rule management to avoid configuration drift.

roadmap.detail: Map existing network zones, identify trust boundaries, and define Zero Trust segmentation policy.
Provision firewall appliances/servers and plan VLAN restructuring.
Deploy pfSense/OPNsense, configure VLANs and firewall policies, set up WireGuard VPN.
Integrate centralized identity (FreeIPA/AD), deploy Wazuh agents, configure IDS/IPS.
Penetration-test segmentation boundaries; validate VPN access scoping and IDS/IPS detection rates against known attack patterns.
Document incident response procedures and finalize security monitoring runbooks.

security.authentication: All access requires authentication against centralized identity; no implicit trust based on network location alone.
security.authorization: Explicit firewall policy per segment, following least-privilege principles.
security.network: Strict VLAN segmentation with default-deny policy between zones.
security.backup: Firewall configuration and Wazuh rule sets backed up and version-controlled.
security.monitoring: Continuous Wazuh-based security event monitoring and IDS/IPS alerting.
security.ha: Redundant firewall pairs (active/passive or active/active) for environments requiring continuous availability.

testing: Segmentation test: verify default-deny policy blocks unauthorized inter-zone traffic.
VPN scoping test: confirm remote users can only reach explicitly authorized segments.
IDS/IPS test: validate detection against known attack signatures/patterns in a controlled test.
Logging test: confirm all access and security events are captured centrally and correlated correctly.
deliverables: Documented Zero Trust network architecture and segmentation policy.
Operational firewall, VPN and IDS/IPS infrastructure.
Centralized security monitoring dashboard (Wazuh).
Incident response and audit documentation.
future: Extension to device-level posture checking before granting access (full Zero Trust device trust).
Integration with the AIOps platform (Project 03) for intelligent security alert correlation.
Multi-factor authentication rollout across all access points.

projects.title: Enterprise Distributed Storage & Data Management System
projects.short: A highly scalable, distributed storage architecture built on Ceph, providing object, block and file storage with replication, quotas and high availability for enterprise and research infrastructure.
projects.challenge: Providing a single storage platform that can serve multiple access patterns (object, block, file) while maintaining data durability as capacity scales across many nodes.
projects.businessValue: Removes single points of failure inherent in traditional monolithic storage arrays and scales capacity/performance by adding nodes rather than forklift upgrades.
objectives: Deploy a distributed storage cluster supporting object, block and file access patterns.
Implement data replication/erasure coding for durability.
Provide per-user/project storage quotas.
Enable centralized, monitored, highly-available storage access.
projects.problem: Traditional single-controller storage arrays create both a capacity ceiling and a single point of failure, and organizations increasingly need to serve multiple access patterns (S3-style object storage for applications, block storage for VMs, file storage for general use) from one coherent platform.
projects.solution: A Ceph cluster providing RADOS as the underlying distributed object store, with CephFS (file), RBD (block) and S3-compatible object gateway access layered on top, replicated across multiple OSD nodes for durability, with ZFS used on individual nodes where local data integrity features are valuable.
projects.users: IT infrastructure teams, application teams needing object/block storage, and general users needing shared file storage with quotas.

businessDetail.operational: Consolidates what might otherwise be several separate storage systems (NAS, SAN, object store) into one unified, centrally managed platform.
businessDetail.cost: Scales by adding commodity storage nodes rather than replacing an entire proprietary array at a capacity ceiling.
businessDetail.productivity: Application teams get self-service S3-compatible object storage without needing a separate cloud storage dependency.
businessDetail.scalability: Designed from the ground up for horizontal scaling — capacity and performance grow by adding OSD nodes.
businessDetail.security: Per-pool/user access controls and quotas prevent any single project from consuming all available capacity.
businessDetail.impact: Provides the general-purpose storage foundation that complements the specialized parallel filesystem (Project 13) used for raw HPC I/O performance.

architecture.overview: A Ceph cluster with monitor nodes (cluster state/quorum), OSD nodes (actual data storage across disks), and manager nodes, exposing RADOS Block Device (RBD) for block storage, CephFS for POSIX file access, and a RADOS Gateway for S3-compatible object storage.
components: Ceph OSDs (object storage daemons) across storage nodes
CephFS Metadata Servers (MDS) for file access
RADOS Gateway (RGW) for S3-compatible object access
ZFS on individual node-local storage where applicable
architecture.dataflow: Client request (object/block/file) → routed to the appropriate Ceph access layer (RGW/RBD/CephFS) → RADOS distributes and replicates the underlying data objects across multiple OSD nodes according to the configured replication/erasure-coding policy → monitors maintain cluster map consistency throughout.
architecture.integration: Can serve as the general-purpose storage backend for the AI platform's document store (Project 01), general file sharing, and VM/container block storage needs across the infrastructure.

stackRationale.why: A mature, widely-deployed distributed storage system supporting object, block and file access from a single underlying cluster, avoiding the need for separate siloed storage systems.
The reliable autonomic distributed object store underlying all of Ceph's access methods, providing self-healing replication/rebalancing.
Gives application teams a familiar, widely-supported object storage API without dependency on a public cloud provider.
Where used at the node level, provides strong local data integrity checks (checksumming) complementing Ceph's cluster-level replication.

hardware.cpu: Moderate core counts per OSD node; Ceph performance scales with both CPU and disk I/O parallelism.
hardware.ram: Significant RAM per OSD node (commonly 4–8GB per OSD daemon as a planning guideline) for cache and metadata performance.
hardware.storage: Multiple disks per OSD node (HDD for capacity tiers, SSD/NVMe for performance tiers or as a cache layer); total capacity planned with replication/erasure-coding overhead factored in.
hardware.networking: 10GbE minimum between OSD nodes; 25GbE+ recommended for larger clusters to avoid replication traffic becoming a bottleneck.
hardware.recommended: Minimum viable production cluster: 3+ monitor nodes (odd number for quorum) and typically a minimum of several OSD nodes for meaningful redundancy.
hardware.note: Exact sizing depends heavily on target capacity, replication factor and performance requirements; figures are general Ceph deployment guidance.

software.os: Linux (Ubuntu Server or Rocky Linux, both well-supported by Ceph).
dependencies: Ceph packages (ceph-mon, ceph-osd, ceph-mgr, ceph-mds, radosgw)
software.databases: Not applicable in the traditional sense — Ceph maintains its own internal cluster map and metadata structures.
software.apis: S3-compatible REST API (via RGW) for object storage; standard POSIX for CephFS; block device interface for RBD.
software.monitoring: Ceph's built-in dashboard plus Prometheus/Grafana integration for cluster health and capacity monitoring.
software.automation: cephadm for orchestrated deployment and lifecycle management of cluster daemons.

roadmap.detail: Determine required capacity, access patterns (object/block/file mix), and replication/erasure-coding policy.
Provision monitor and OSD nodes with appropriate disk and network configuration.
Deploy Ceph via cephadm, configure monitors, OSDs, and initial pools.
Enable CephFS, RBD and RGW access layers as needed; configure per-project quotas.
Run I/O benchmarks per access pattern; validate failure recovery by simulating OSD/node loss.
Document capacity management procedures and finalize monitoring/alerting thresholds.

security.authentication: Ceph's cephx authentication protocol for inter-daemon and client authentication; RGW integrates with standard S3-style access keys.
security.authorization: Per-pool and per-user capability restrictions limiting access scope.
security.network: Separate public and cluster (replication) network segments recommended for performance and security isolation.
security.backup: Cross-site replication or periodic snapshots/exports for disaster recovery beyond in-cluster redundancy.
security.monitoring: Continuous cluster health monitoring (OSD status, placement group health, capacity thresholds).
security.dr: Documented procedures for OSD/node failure recovery and, where configured, multi-site disaster recovery.
security.ha: Inherent high availability through replication/erasure coding and monitor quorum; no single node failure should cause data loss or unavailability when properly sized.

testing: Durability test: simulate OSD/node failure and confirm automatic rebalancing/recovery without data loss.
Performance test: benchmark object/block/file I/O throughput against target workload profiles.
Quota test: verify per-project/user storage quotas are correctly enforced.
Failover test: validate monitor quorum behavior when a monitor node becomes unavailable.
deliverables: Operational distributed storage cluster supporting object, block and file access.
Documented capacity and quota management procedures.
Monitoring dashboards for cluster health and capacity.
Benchmark report validating performance against target workloads.
future: Multi-site replication for geographic disaster recovery.
Tiered storage (hot NVMe / cold HDD) policy automation.
Integration with Kubernetes via the Ceph CSI driver for container-native storage.

projects.title: HPC Parallel File System & High-Speed Storage
projects.short: A parallel storage infrastructure purpose-built for demanding HPC and AI workloads requiring very high aggregate throughput and concurrent access from many compute nodes.
projects.challenge: Delivering the sustained high-bandwidth, low-latency I/O that hundreds of compute nodes reading/writing simultaneously require — a workload pattern conventional NFS storage struggles to serve efficiently.
projects.businessValue: Prevents storage I/O from becoming the bottleneck that limits HPC/AI cluster performance, protecting the return on investment in compute hardware.
objectives: Deploy a parallel file system capable of serving high concurrent I/O from many compute nodes.
Use NVMe/SSD caching to accelerate hot data access.
Leverage RDMA networking (InfiniBand/100GbE) to minimize I/O latency.
Benchmark and validate achieved throughput against HPC workload requirements.
projects.problem: Conventional NFS storage uses a single (or small number of) server(s) to serve all clients, which becomes a severe bottleneck when hundreds of HPC compute nodes need to read/write large datasets simultaneously — the storage system itself, not the compute, ends up limiting job performance.
projects.solution: A parallel file system (Lustre or BeeGFS) that stripes data across many storage servers and targets simultaneously, allowing aggregate throughput to scale with the number of storage nodes, connected via RDMA networking (InfiniBand or RoCE over 100GbE) to minimize latency, with NVMe/SSD used as a caching tier for frequently accessed data.
projects.users: HPC compute clusters (Project 04), AI training clusters (Project 02), and any workload requiring very high aggregate storage throughput.

businessDetail.operational: Eliminates the storage bottleneck pattern common with single-server NFS under heavy concurrent HPC access.
businessDetail.cost: Higher upfront cost than simple NFS storage, justified when compute cluster scale makes storage I/O the limiting factor on overall cluster utilization.
businessDetail.productivity: Faster data access directly translates to shorter job completion times for I/O-intensive HPC/AI workloads.
businessDetail.scalability: Throughput scales near-linearly by adding more storage server/target nodes, unlike single-server NFS.
businessDetail.security: Access control integrated with the same centralized identity used across the HPC cluster.
businessDetail.impact: A deliberate complement to the general-purpose Ceph storage platform (Project 12) — this system is specifically for raw HPC I/O performance, not general file sharing.

architecture.overview: A parallel file system architecture with metadata servers (handling file/directory metadata) separated from object storage servers (handling actual data), allowing both metadata operations and data throughput to scale independently, striped across many storage targets accessed concurrently.
components: Object Storage Servers / Storage Nodes (OSS in Lustre terms, storage servers in BeeGFS)
architecture.dataflow: Compute node issues a file I/O request → metadata server resolves file layout/striping information → compute node communicates directly and in parallel with multiple storage servers/targets for the actual data transfer → RDMA networking allows this to happen with minimal CPU overhead and latency.
architecture.integration: Mounted directly by HPC cluster compute nodes (Project 04) and AI training cluster nodes (Project 02) as their primary high-performance working storage, distinct from the general-purpose Ceph platform used for other storage needs.

stackRationale.why: The most widely deployed parallel file system in large-scale HPC/supercomputing environments, with a long track record at extreme scale.
Generally simpler to deploy and manage than Lustre while still providing strong parallel I/O performance, often preferred for mid-scale deployments.
Essential for parallel file systems to achieve their full performance potential, since standard TCP/IP networking overhead would otherwise limit achievable throughput and latency.
Accelerates access to frequently-used ('hot') datasets without requiring the entire filesystem capacity to be built on the most expensive storage media.

hardware.cpu: Moderate CPU requirements on storage servers; metadata servers benefit from strong single-thread performance for metadata operation latency.
hardware.ram: Substantial RAM on metadata servers for caching file system metadata; storage servers benefit from RAM for data caching.
hardware.storage: NVMe/SSD for caching/hot tier; high-capacity HDD or SSD arrays for the bulk capacity tier, striped across many storage targets.
hardware.networking: RDMA-capable network fabric (InfiniBand or 100GbE with RoCE) is effectively mandatory to realize the performance benefits of a parallel file system.
hardware.recommended: Minimum practical deployment: dedicated metadata server(s) plus multiple storage server nodes; scales by adding storage servers for both capacity and throughput.
hardware.note: Achieved throughput is highly dependent on network fabric, storage media and node count; IOR benchmarking against the specific deployment is required for validated figures.

software.os: Linux with vendor/project-specific kernel patches or modules as required by Lustre; BeeGFS has broader generic kernel compatibility.
services: Client mount services on compute nodes
software.databases: Not applicable in the traditional sense — file system metadata is managed internally by Lustre/BeeGFS.
software.apis: POSIX filesystem interface for compute node access; administrative CLI tools for management.
software.monitoring: Filesystem-specific monitoring tools plus integration into the broader HPC monitoring platform (Project 05).
software.automation: Ansible for consistent deployment of metadata/storage server roles.

roadmap.detail: Determine target aggregate throughput, capacity, and compatible RDMA networking fabric.
Provision metadata and storage server hardware with RDMA-capable networking.
Install and configure Lustre or BeeGFS metadata and storage services.
Mount the parallel file system on HPC/AI cluster compute nodes; configure NVMe caching tier.
Run IOR benchmarks to validate aggregate throughput and metadata operation performance against targets.
Document capacity planning and finalize monitoring/alerting for storage server health.

security.authentication: Integrated with the HPC cluster's centralized identity for client access control.
security.authorization: Directory/file-level POSIX permissions, consistent with standard HPC storage access models.
security.network: Storage fabric isolated on its own RDMA network segment, separate from general management traffic.
security.backup: Given this is typically scratch/working storage, backup policy often differs from archival storage — data is commonly expected to be copied to longer-term storage (Project 12/14) rather than relied upon as permanent.
security.monitoring: Storage server health and throughput monitoring integrated with the HPC monitoring platform.
security.dr: Documented procedure for metadata/storage server recovery; data durability strategy should be explicit given parallel filesystems often prioritize performance over long-term redundancy.
security.ha: Metadata server redundancy (where supported) to avoid a single point of failure for the entire filesystem.

testing: IOR benchmark test: validate aggregate read/write throughput against target performance goals.
Metadata performance test: measure file creation/stat operation rates under concurrent load.
Failover test: validate behavior when a storage server becomes unavailable (data availability depends on configured redundancy).
Integration test: confirm HPC/AI cluster compute nodes can mount and use the filesystem under real job workloads.
deliverables: Operational parallel file system integrated with HPC/AI compute clusters.
IOR benchmark report validating achieved throughput and latency.
Documented capacity planning and data lifecycle policy (scratch vs archival).
Monitoring dashboards for storage server health.
future: Automated data lifecycle management moving cold data to the Ceph platform (Project 12) or backup system (Project 14).
Expansion of the NVMe caching tier as hot-data working sets grow.
Evaluation of newer parallel filesystem technologies as they mature.
projects.comparisonNote: Lustre and BeeGFS differ from conventional NFS storage in a fundamental way: NFS serves all clients from a single server (or a small HA pair), creating a throughput ceiling, while Lustre and BeeGFS stripe data across many independent storage servers so that aggregate throughput scales with the number of servers added. BeeGFS is generally considered simpler to deploy and administer; Lustre has a longer track record at the largest supercomputing scales. Both require RDMA-capable networking to realize their full performance potential, which NFS does not typically demand.

projects.title: Enterprise Backup, Disaster Recovery & Business Continuity Platform
projects.short: A reliable enterprise data protection platform providing automated, incremental backups, snapshot management, off-site replication and documented disaster recovery procedures.
projects.challenge: Guaranteeing that backups are not just taken but are actually restorable, immutable against ransomware/accidental deletion, and meet defined recovery time/point objectives.
projects.businessValue: Protects the organization against data loss from hardware failure, human error, or ransomware, and provides a documented, tested path back to operation after a disaster.
objectives: Implement automated, incremental backup across critical systems.
Maintain snapshot-based point-in-time recovery options.
Replicate backups off-site for disaster resilience.
Define and validate RPO/RTO targets through regular recovery testing.
projects.problem: Many organizations run backups without ever testing restores, without off-site copies protecting against site-level disasters, and without immutability protecting against ransomware encrypting both production data and its backups — meaning the backup system fails exactly when it's needed most.
projects.solution: A layered backup architecture: ZFS snapshots for fast, frequent local point-in-time recovery; Proxmox Backup Server/BorgBackup/Restic for deduplicated, encrypted incremental backups; rsync and S3-compatible storage for off-site replication; and a disciplined, documented policy of regular recovery testing against defined RPO/RTO targets.
projects.users: IT infrastructure teams responsible for data protection, and organizational leadership requiring assurance of business continuity capability.

businessDetail.operational: Converts backup from a theoretical safety net into a verified, regularly-tested capability.
businessDetail.cost: Built on open-source tooling (BorgBackup, Restic, Proxmox Backup Server), minimizing licensing cost relative to commercial backup appliances.
businessDetail.productivity: Fast snapshot-based recovery for common accidental-deletion scenarios avoids lengthy full-restore processes for minor incidents.
businessDetail.scalability: Incremental, deduplicated backups scale storage efficiently as data volume grows over time.
businessDetail.security: Immutable backup strategies protect against ransomware that attempts to encrypt or delete backup data alongside production data.
businessDetail.impact: Provides the final safety net underpinning every other infrastructure project in this portfolio — AI platforms, HPC clusters, EDA design data and storage systems all depend on this layer being genuinely trustworthy.

architecture.overview: A multi-tier backup strategy: frequent ZFS snapshots provide fast local recovery points, incremental deduplicated backups (via Proxmox Backup Server/BorgBackup/Restic) provide space-efficient longer-term retention, and off-site replication (rsync/S3) protects against site-level disasters.
components: ZFS snapshot schedule on primary storage
Proxmox Backup Server / BorgBackup / Restic for incremental backups
Off-site replication target (rsync destination or S3-compatible storage)
Immutability configuration (where supported) to resist ransomware/deletion
architecture.dataflow: Scheduled ZFS snapshots capture frequent local recovery points → periodic backup jobs (Borg/Restic/PBS) create deduplicated, encrypted incremental backups of critical data → backups replicated off-site via rsync or to S3-compatible storage → monitoring confirms each job's success and alerts on failure → recovery tests periodically validate that restores actually work.
architecture.integration: Protects data from every other project in the portfolio — AI document stores, EDA design libraries, Ceph/parallel filesystem data, and general enterprise data all flow into this backup layer according to their defined retention policy.

stackRationale.why: Near-instantaneous, space-efficient point-in-time recovery points ideal for quickly reverting recent accidental changes without a full restore.
Deduplicated, encrypted incremental backup tools that are efficient with both storage space and bandwidth for off-site transfer.
Purpose-built for efficient VM/container backup with deduplication, particularly valuable if the infrastructure is virtualized on Proxmox.
Provides a flexible off-site target that can be self-hosted (e.g. on the Ceph platform from Project 12) or a third-party service, depending on organizational preference.

hardware.cpu: Moderate CPU for backup job processing (deduplication/compression/encryption are CPU-sensitive operations).
hardware.ram: 16–64GB depending on deduplication index size and data volume.
hardware.storage: Backup target storage sized to retention policy, typically 2-4x+ the protected data volume depending on retention depth and deduplication ratio achieved.
hardware.networking: Sufficient bandwidth for backup windows to complete within policy; off-site replication bandwidth sized to data change rate (not full dataset size, due to incremental backups).
hardware.recommended: Dedicated backup server(s) separate from production systems, with off-site replication target physically/logically isolated from the primary site.
hardware.note: Storage and bandwidth sizing depend heavily on data volume, change rate and retention policy; figures are general planning guidance.

software.os: Linux (Debian-based for Proxmox Backup Server; general Linux for BorgBackup/Restic).
services: Backup scheduling service (cron/systemd timers or PBS's built-in scheduler)
software.databases: Proxmox Backup Server maintains its own internal chunk store/index; BorgBackup/Restic maintain repository-local indexes.
software.apis: Proxmox Backup Server API for programmatic backup management; CLI-driven for BorgBackup/Restic.
software.monitoring: Backup job success/failure alerting integrated with the broader monitoring platform (Project 05).
software.automation: Scheduled, automated backup jobs with no reliance on manual execution; automated recovery test scheduling where feasible.

roadmap.detail: Classify data by criticality and define RPO/RTO targets per data category.
Provision backup server(s) and off-site replication target infrastructure.
Deploy ZFS snapshot schedules, configure BorgBackup/Restic/PBS jobs for all critical systems.
Configure off-site replication and immutability settings; integrate backup monitoring/alerting.
Perform scheduled recovery tests validating actual restore success against defined RPO/RTO targets.
Document the full backup/recovery runbook and finalize the recurring recovery-test schedule.

security.authentication: Backup infrastructure access restricted to designated backup administrators.
security.authorization: Least-privilege access to backup repositories; separation of duties between backup administration and production system administration where feasible.
security.network: Backup traffic isolated on its own network segment where practical.
security.backup: This project is itself the backup layer; its own configuration (job definitions, schedules) is version-controlled.
security.monitoring: Automated alerting on backup job failure, with escalation if failures are not resolved within a defined window.
security.dr: This project directly implements disaster recovery capability for the rest of the infrastructure; its own DR plan covers backup server/configuration loss.
security.ha: Off-site replication inherently provides site-level resilience; backup server redundancy optional depending on criticality.

testing: Restore test: periodically perform full restores and validate data integrity against source.
RPO validation: confirm actual backup frequency meets the defined recovery point objective per data category.
RTO validation: measure actual time-to-restore against the defined recovery time objective.
Immutability test: confirm backups cannot be altered/deleted within their configured retention window, even with compromised production credentials.
deliverables: Operational automated backup system covering all critical infrastructure.
Off-site replicated backup copies meeting defined disaster recovery requirements.
Documented, tested recovery runbook with validated RPO/RTO figures.
Ongoing recovery test schedule and reporting.
future: Automated, orchestrated full-site disaster recovery drills.
Extension of immutability policies across all backup tiers.
Integration with the AIOps platform (Project 03) for intelligent backup failure triage.
